items.t: Dating again? What older adults should know about sexual health and protection
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Dating, intimacy and connection can be an important part of emotional and physical well-being for older adults. That includes people who are divorced, widowed, remarried or dating again for the first time in decades. The Aging Untold experts are addressing the topics of sexual health, how it has changed over the years and how to stay protected. items.x: (Gray News) - Ground cinnamon is being recalled in 14 states ahead of the holiday season. SLR Food Distribution Inc said it’s voluntarily recalling Wise Wife Brand Ground Cinnamon because it could be contaminated with elevated levels of lead, according to a recall alert. The affected cinnamon was sold in retail and grocery stores between Sept. 8, 2025, and June 28, 2026, in Connecticut, Indiana, Kansas, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, North Carolina, Nebraska, New York, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Texas, Virginia and Wisconsin. According to the recall notice, lead exposure can impact nearly every bodily system, with effects depending on dosage, duration, and an individual’s age and weight. items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Caregiving promises are sometimes made during emotional moments. When a loved one says, “I’ll never put you in a home,” or “You can always live with me,” the words may come from love, but health, safety, money and caregiver capacity can change over time. Her pain was on her back and flank. “Not something I could see, not something I could reach, but just an intense amount of burning. And then it came around,” she said. items.t: Better than blood? Researcher says new discovery could help save lives
items.x: KANSAS CITY, Mo. ( InvestigateTV ) — A doctor and research scientist at the University of Missouri-Kansas City said he has discovered a potential alternative to blood transfusions for people with severe blood loss. He calls the treatment “better than blood.” When someone experiences severe trauma, such as a car crash or gunshot wound, they risk bleeding to death. Blood transfusions are currently the best treatment to try to stop severe blood loss, also known as hemorrhagic shock. items.t: How caregivers can keep dignity intact when conversations get tense
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Stress can turn into sharp words when you are a caregiver for someone you love. The Aging Untold experts are sharing advice on how to communicate in a way that keeps dignity intact, builds cooperation and helps caregivers reset when a conversation escalates. Step away before things escalate “Sam” Cradduck, a gerontologist, said the first move to make when it feels like a conversation is about to escalate is to leave the room. “You have to step away. You really do,” Cradduck said. “You’ve got to let yourself calm down.” Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said caregivers can take that step by removing themselves or getting help. “If you’re fantasizing about escaping, or noticing the yellow flags like you’re starting to get hot, shaky, your jaw’s tense, that’s a good time to go, ‘OK, my nervous system is at its limit,’” Ambrose said. items.x: The above video is our WITN+ livestream and may not reflect the content in this story. KINSTON, N.C. (WITN) - Kinston police arrested a man on fraud charges. Police say officers were called to First Citizens Bank for a fraud in progress yesterday. Bank employees reported that a person was trying to withdraw $10,000 from a customer’s account using fraudulent identification. Police confirmed the identification was false and arrested 64-year-old Willie White. Police say further investigation linked White to another incident at the same bank, during which he withdrew $10,000 from another victim’s account using the holder’s ID and personal information. White was charged with two counts of obtaining property by false pretenses, two counts of identity theft and possession of stolen property. He was booked into the Lenoir County Jail.

items.t: What to look for in a clinical trial and why older adults should be included
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Clinical trials can be a proactive way to explore new treatments, but studies show older adults are often left out of them, even though many conditions affect older adults more often. The Aging Untold experts hosts are discussing what to look for when choosing a study and how to decide whether to take part. Start with the question the trial is trying to answer Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said the first step is to change the question you ask. “I think the first thing we have to do is not think about, ‘Can this clinical trial help me?’ but ‘What is this clinical trial trying to answer?’” Rogers said. “That’s what most of these trials are about.” A trial is not a last resort Rogers said many people see clinical trials as a last resort. “I think a lot of people think that it’s a last resort option, that you don’t have anything else, when in fact one of th

Before moving in with her mother, Cathie lived in Richmond, Virginia, and had a career in a technical field. items.t: NEW INFO: Fired Chocowinity town clerk indicted in embezzlement investigation
items.x: CHOCOWINITY, N.C. (WITN) - The SBI has shared more details into their investigation into a former Chocowinity town clerk. The SBI says Lauren Hoggard voided utility bills for her own residences instead of paying them, overpaid her own payroll and took cash that should have been deposited into the town’s bank account. Hoggard was indicted and arrested on three counts of embezzlement by a public officer or trustee. According to the indictment, Hoggard embezzled up to $100,000 from the town from 2022 to 2024 while serving as clerk. The court will set her Superior Court date later. WITN learned Hoggard was fired on August 21, 2024. She replaced Joy McRoy in July 2022 after McRoy was also let go. McRoy was previously indicted on accusations of embezzling more than half a million dollars from the town over seven years. Hoggard has posted a $135,000 secured bond.

items.t: Saving Graces 4 Felines: Meet Princess
items.x: GREENVILLE, N.C. (WITN) - WITN is working with Saving Graces 4 Felines to find cats and kittens ‘fur-ever’ homes. Meet Princess. Get ready to treat Princess like royalty! She’s one of four kittens rescued from a colony of community cats. Princess has blossomed into a sweet and playful girl who loves other cats and kittens. She purrs the second she sees a person and is always seeking attention! If you are interested in Princess or her three siblings, please reach out to Saving Graces 4 Felines. Apply to adopt at savinggraces4felines.org. The adoption fee is $95 in cash, and a good vet reference is required. Saving Graces 4 Felines’ adoptable cats are spayed or neutered before adoption is finalized. They have been tested for feline leukemia and FIV, are up to date on vaccines, and have been treated for worms and fleas. They have also been microchipped.

items.t: Older adults who stop driving face transportation gaps, experts say
items.x: KANSAS CITY ( InvestigateTV ) — As people age and their health changes, families can face the question of when a loved one should stop driving. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration reports older drivers are more likely than younger drivers to be involved in a car accident. items.t: Doctor says time outdoors can support physical and mental health
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Spending time in nature can be a healthy reset, according to a doctor who also practices wilderness medicine. Dr. Nathaniel Mann, a Prisma Health emergency doctor, said time spent outdoors is one of the most powerful treatments he has seen, and he supports prescribing it. “Humans, we really didn’t evolve to live in these big structured communities with all the traffic and lights and noise. Doctor cites human history outdoors Mann spent two years traveling the world, practicing medicine in remote environments. Across his years in medicine, he has found that being outside is one of the most powerful treatments. items.t: Grand Ledge bringing agricultural education back after nearly 40 years

Now think about that in a pathway, in a nerve pathway in your body,” Cradduck said. Her pain was on her back and flank. “Not something I could see, not something I could reach, but just an intense amount of burning. And then it came around,” she said. ( InvestigateTV ) — A doctor and research scientist at the University of Missouri-Kansas City said he has discovered a potential alternative to blood transfusions for people with severe blood loss. items.t: Missing Texas man found deceased
items.x: FAYETTE COUNTY, W.Va. (WVVA) - A missing Texas man has been found deceased in Fayette County as a result of a dirt bike crash. Sheriff Jess McMullen said the Sheriff’s Department started searching for Paul Alexander Kirkland, 35, of Caddo Mills, Texas, Thursday morning after he was reported missing. His body was found near the Prince Train Station by a CSX employee. The preliminary investigation indicates Kirkland was traveling northbound on Route 41 on a dirt bike sometime Wednesday night when he lost control coming out of a curve near the train tracks. The bike struck a tree, ejecting Kirkland, who sustained fatal head and neck injuries. He was not wearing a helmet. The crash went undiscovered overnight because the rider and debris were located well off the roadway. The incident remains under investigation.

Research published by the National Library of Medicine shows drawing and painting can sometimes stimulate memories in people with dementia and other neurological diseases. On the day of the interview, Cathie was painting a bottle purple, the color of Alzheimer’s awareness. Before moving in with her mother, Cathie lived in Richmond, Virginia, and had a career in a technical field. items.t: Staying dry through Halloween, showers possible to start November
items.x: Once again, the stretch of a repeated dry weather pattern will continue as we head into this upcoming weekend. Moving throughout the day Friday, our high temperatures will rebound nicely as we see high pressure nudge its way back into the region. With the exception of cooler temperatures, you really couldn’t ask for much out of a late October day as temperatures make a run at the upper 60’s and the low 70’s. We will see a few clouds continue to build as we head into the overnight hours. Those clouds continue to build as we head into Halloween on Saturday with temperatures being stunted slightly into the low and middle 60’s. The cloud cover does linger around heading into the day on Sunday, it is possible for a few showers to sneak its way into the region, although anything that does make it to the ground will have to overcome dry air at the surface. items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Caregiving promises are sometimes made during emotional moments. When a loved one says, “I’ll never put you in a home,” or “You can always live with me,” the words may come from love, but health, safety, money and caregiver capacity can change over time. The Aging Untold experts explain why families may feel guilt or pressure later and what to say instead. Why promises can create pressure Families often make promises before they have talked through what caregiving could involve, Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, said. “They haven’t looked at the reality and talked about the reality at first,” O’Rourke said. “You know, ‘I’ll take care of you.’ But if these certain things happen, we’re going to have to have another conversation.” She said the questions can be practical: Can we afford the care? It’s an infection in the nerve, essentially. It is nerve pain at the highest level,” Cradduck said. She compared it to a toothache. “You know how intense a toothache is. Now think about that in a pathway, in a nerve pathway in your body,” Cradduck said. Her pain was on her back and flank. “Not something I could see, not something I could reach, but just an intense amount of burning. And then it came around,” she said. He calls the treatment “better than blood.” When someone experiences severe trauma, such as a car crash or gunshot wound, they risk bleeding to death. items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Stress can turn into sharp words when you are a caregiver for someone you love. The Aging Untold experts are sharing advice on how to communicate in a way that keeps dignity intact, builds cooperation and helps caregivers reset when a conversation escalates. items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Clinical trials can be a proactive way to explore new treatments, but studies show older adults are often left out of them, even though many conditions affect older adults more often. items.t: $39.7 million in federal funding announced for rural Missouri hospitals
items.x: MISSOURI (Heartland News) - The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services announced $39.7 million in investments intended to modernize rural healthcare services and expanded healthcare access in Missouri. According to a news release, the Rural Health Transformation Program(RHTP) will help pay for 26 rural healthcare providers to renovate, equip, or repurpose existing facilities. Officials say the RHTP is intended to increase primary care options, as well as expand services like labor and delivery, MRI, behavioral health, and substance abuse care. “By supporting locally driven solutions, we are helping rural communities build a stronger health care system that improves outcomes for Missouri families today and for generations to come,” said Missouri Governor Mike Kehoe. For more information about the RHTP, visit the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services website .

items.t: When ‘I’ll never put you in a home’ meets real-life caregiving
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Caregiving promises are sometimes made during emotional moments. When a loved one says, “I’ll never put you in a home,” or “You can always live with me,” the words may come from love, but health, safety, money and caregiver capacity can change over time. The Aging Untold experts explain why families may feel guilt or pressure later and what to say instead. Why promises can create pressure Families often make promises before they have talked through what caregiving could involve, Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, said. “They haven’t looked at the reality and talked about the reality at first,” O’Rourke said. “You know, ‘I’ll take care of you.’ But if these certain things happen, we’re going to have to have another conversation.” She said the questions can be practical: Can we afford the care? items.t: Better than blood? Researcher says new discovery could help save lives
items.x: KANSAS CITY, Mo. ( InvestigateTV ) — A doctor and research scientist at the University of Missouri-Kansas City said he has discovered a potential alternative to blood transfusions for people with severe blood loss. He calls the treatment “better than blood.” When someone experiences severe trauma, such as a car crash or gunshot wound, they risk bleeding to death. Blood transfusions are currently the best treatment to try to stop severe blood loss, also known as hemorrhagic shock. items.t: How caregivers can keep dignity intact when conversations get tense
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Stress can turn into sharp words when you are a caregiver for someone you love. The Aging Untold experts are sharing advice on how to communicate in a way that keeps dignity intact, builds cooperation and helps caregivers reset when a conversation escalates. Step away before things escalate “Sam” Cradduck, a gerontologist, said the first move to make when it feels like a conversation is about to escalate is to leave the room. “You have to step away. items.t: Snake Road migration closure extended into November
items.x: UNION COUNTY, Ill. (Heartland News) - The U.S. Forest Service announced that the Snake Road will remain open until the first week of November. The U.S. Forest Service announced that the Snake Road will now close on November 5. According to Shawnee National Forest authorities, the unseasonably warm weather is causing the snake migration season to lengthen. Each fall the snakes migrate from their summer habitat in LaRue Swamp to their winter habitat in the limestone bluffs. While the closure means motor vehicles cannot use the road, nature lovers can still walk the snake road to witness the migration first hand. For more information about the Snake Road hike, visit the U.S. Department of Agriculture website .

Kimberly Cheatham, owner of Kreative Kimistry in Anderson, has joined the Pink Palmetto Project, an effort by the South Carolina Cancer Alliance focusing on breast and cervical cancer education. Cheatham said her clients often get personal with her. “They confide in me when they don’t even feel comfortable telling their families things and their friends, because they know that I have a connection to them,” Cheatham said. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration reports older drivers are more likely than younger drivers to be involved in a car accident. items.t: Man sentenced to 20 years in prison after Georgetown investigation

items.x: GEORGETOWN COUNTY, SC (WMBF) - A shrimp boat that washed ashore in Myrtle Beach during Hurricane Ian in 2022 needed a Coast Guard rescue again Wednesday. The crew of the Shayna Michelle, a commercial shrimp boat, radioed the Coast Guard around 12:50 p.m. to report the boat was taking on water and was stuck on a Winyah Bay jetty in Georgetown County. Using a helicopter, the Coast Guard said it rescued five people and a dog. Crews released video of the rescue. Credit: Coast Guard “We train to a standard and our crew worked incredibly well together on this challenging rescue,” Lt. Hunter Shortly, an aircraft commander with the Coast Guard, said. “It was difficult to access the shrimping vessel with its many wires and cables, but our rescue swimmer did a phenomenal job of getting all aboard to safety.” No injuries were reported, and the cause is under investigation. items.t: When ‘I’ll never put you in a home’ meets real-life caregiving
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Caregiving promises are sometimes made during emotional moments. When a loved one says, “I’ll never put you in a home,” or “You can always live with me,” the words may come from love, but health, safety, money and caregiver capacity can change over time. The Aging Untold experts explain why families may feel guilt or pressure later and what to say instead. Why promises can create pressure Families often make promises before they have talked through what caregiving could involve, Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, said. “They haven’t looked at the reality and talked about the reality at first,” O’Rourke said. “You know, ‘I’ll take care of you.’ But if these certain things happen, we’re going to have to have another conversation.” She said the questions can be practical: Can we afford the care? items.t: ‘Bad houseguest’ in the attic: What to know about shingles symptoms and treatments
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Many people think the first sign of shingles is a bad rash, but it can start with intense pain in the body. ‘Intense amount of burning’ Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said she had shingles twice and it was tied to an autoimmune condition, and described the pain as burning. “It burned. It’s an infection in the nerve, essentially. It is nerve pain at the highest level,” Cradduck said. She compared it to a toothache. “You know how intense a toothache is. Now think about that in a pathway, in a nerve pathway in your body,” Cradduck said. Her pain was on her back and flank. “Not something I could see, not something I could reach, but just an intense amount of burning. And then it came around,” she said. items.x: GEORGETOWN COUNTY, SC (WMBF) - The Georgetown County Sheriff’s Office says the search for a missing Pawleys Island-area man is over. In a Friday update, a spokesperson for the sheriff’s office confirmed Christopher Harms, 57, was found dead. The sheriff’s office said it was “saddened to report” the news and that it was “not the outcome we wanted or expected.” Deputies asked the public for help finding Harms on Tuesday after he stopped communicating with his family on Oct. 23. The sheriff’s office thanked the public for its help in the search. Deputies are asking the public to respect the family’s request for time to grieve in private. items.t: Better than blood? Researcher says new discovery could help save lives
items.x: KANSAS CITY, Mo. ( InvestigateTV ) — A doctor and research scientist at the University of Missouri-Kansas City said he has discovered a potential alternative to blood transfusions for people with severe blood loss. He calls the treatment “better than blood.” When someone experiences severe trauma, such as a car crash or gunshot wound, they risk bleeding to death. Blood transfusions are currently the best treatment to try to stop severe blood loss, also known as hemorrhagic shock. How the discovery happened Dr. Cuthbert Simpkins, founder of Vivacelle Bio, said he was running an experiment he thought would fail. “But it didn’t fail.” For years, Simpkins, who is now a surgery professor at the UKMC School of Medicine, had been trying to find an answer for septic shock and focused his research on blood experiments. The number is now the highest early turnout for a gubernatorial election since the state first began offering early voting in 2022. items.t: How caregivers can keep dignity intact when conversations get tense
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Stress can turn into sharp words when you are a caregiver for someone you love. The Aging Untold experts are sharing advice on how to communicate in a way that keeps dignity intact, builds cooperation and helps caregivers reset when a conversation escalates. Step away before things escalate “Sam” Cradduck, a gerontologist, said the first move to make when it feels like a conversation is about to escalate is to leave the room. “You have to step away. You really do,” Cradduck said. “You’ve got to let yourself calm down.” Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said caregivers can take that step by removing themselves or getting help. “If you’re fantasizing about escaping, or noticing the yellow flags like you’re starting to get hot, shaky, your jaw’s tense, that’s a good time to go, ‘OK, my nervous system is at its limit,’” Ambrose said. items.t: What to look for in a clinical trial and why older adults should be included
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Clinical trials can be a proactive way to explore new treatments, but studies show older adults are often left out of them, even though many conditions affect older adults more often. The Aging Untold experts hosts are discussing what to look for when choosing a study and how to decide whether to take part. items.t: Look for new notices at SC restaurants: Imported shrimp must now be disclosed
items.x: COLUMBIA, SC (WMBF) - South Carolina restaurants that serve imported shrimp must now tell customers. The new law took effect Wednesday. Restaurants that serve imported shrimp must post a notice on their menu, if they have one, and on a sign at the main entrance. The notice must say that some items “may contain foreign imported shrimp” and tell customers to ask for more information. Restaurants that serve only imported shrimp must say some items “contain foreign imported shrimp.” Restaurants that break the law first get a warning from the state Department of Agriculture and have three days to fix the problem. A second or later violation can bring a fine of $100 to $5,000 for each day. The law comes after several Lowcountry restaurants were accused of advertising imported shrimp as local. items.t: Bringing cancer screening conversations to the salon chair
items.x: ANDRESON, S.C. ( InvestigateTV ) - Do you only go to the doctor when you have an ache or feel sick? For many women that answer can be “yes.” A 2025 survey said that every one in six women say they missed or may have missed a routine cancer screening within the past year. A South Carolina salon is partnering with a statewide health initiative to have important conversations about cancer screening with clients. Kimberly Cheatham, owner of Kreative Kimistry in Anderson, has joined the Pink Palmetto Project, an effort by the South Carolina Cancer Alliance focusing on breast and cervical cancer education. Cheatham said her clients often get personal with her. “They confide in me when they don’t even feel comfortable telling their families things and their friends, because they know that I have a connection to them,” Cheatham said. items.x: WILMINGTON, N.C. ( InvestigateTV ) — Some doctors and caregivers are using art to help people with memory loss stay calm, engaged and connected. Research published by the National Library of Medicine shows drawing and painting can sometimes stimulate memories in people with dementia and other neurological diseases. Mother and daughter paint together June Lederle and her daughter, Cathie Lederle, create artwork at a table in their Wilmington home most days. On the day of the interview, Cathie was painting a bottle purple, the color of Alzheimer’s awareness. Before moving in with her mother, Cathie lived in Richmond, Virginia, and had a career in a technical field. Crew responded to the first crash near North Cashua Drive and Wall Street on Thursday at 7:20 p.m. The crash involved a bicyclist, and it was later announced that the bicyclist died on the scene of the crash, according to Master Trooper Mitchell Ridgeway. A Kia Sorento was traveling North and hit the person on the bike, who was also traveling in the same direction, Ridgeway says. items.t: Older adults who stop driving face transportation gaps, experts say
items.x: KANSAS CITY ( InvestigateTV ) — As people age and their health changes, families can face the question of when a loved one should stop driving. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration reports older drivers are more likely than younger drivers to be involved in a car accident. items.t: Doctor says time outdoors can support physical and mental health
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Spending time in nature can be a healthy reset, according to a doctor who also practices wilderness medicine. Dr. Nathaniel Mann, a Prisma Health emergency doctor, said time spent outdoors is one of the most powerful treatments he has seen, and he supports prescribing it. “Humans, we really didn’t evolve to live in these big structured communities with all the traffic and lights and noise. Doctor cites human history outdoors Mann spent two years traveling the world, practicing medicine in remote environments. Across his years in medicine, he has found that being outside is one of the most powerful treatments. items.t: Waco mother arrested after toddler found wandering parking lot, police say
items.x: WACO, Texas (KWTX) - Waco Police arrested a woman after leaving her 8-year-old and 2-year-old children alone at home for 8-9 hours while she was at work, according to an arrest affidavit. Curtisha Marshall, 32, was arrested after her 2-year-old child was found wandering in an apartment complex parking lot. According to the affidavit, officers discovered that the 2-year-old and an 8-year-old had been left alone at Marshall’s apartment. Marshall had been at work since 2 p.m. and did not arrive home until approximately 11 p.m., leaving the children unattended for 8-9 hours, the affidavit states. In an interview with CPS, the 8-year-old confirmed that their mother left them home alone all day. items.t: How caregivers can keep dignity intact when conversations get tense
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Stress can turn into sharp words when you are a caregiver for someone you love. The Aging Untold experts are sharing advice on how to communicate in a way that keeps dignity intact, builds cooperation and helps caregivers reset when a conversation escalates. Step away before things escalate “Sam” Cradduck, a gerontologist, said the first move to make when it feels like a conversation is about to escalate is to leave the room. “You have to step away. You really do,” Cradduck said. “You’ve got to let yourself calm down.” Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said caregivers can take that step by removing themselves or getting help. “If you’re fantasizing about escaping, or noticing the yellow flags like you’re starting to get hot, shaky, your jaw’s tense, that’s a good time to go, ‘OK, my nervous system is at its limit,’” Ambrose said. items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Clinical trials can be a proactive way to explore new treatments, but studies show older adults are often left out of them, even though many conditions affect older adults more often. The Aging Untold experts hosts are discussing what to look for when choosing a study and how to decide whether to take part. items.x: ANDRESON, S.C. ( InvestigateTV ) - Do you only go to the doctor when you have an ache or feel sick? For many women that answer can be “yes.” A 2025 survey said that every one in six women say they missed or may have missed a routine cancer screening within the past year. A South Carolina salon is partnering with a statewide health initiative to have important conversations about cancer screening with clients. Kimberly Cheatham, owner of Kreative Kimistry in Anderson, has joined the Pink Palmetto Project, an effort by the South Carolina Cancer Alliance focusing on breast and cervical cancer education. items.x: WILMINGTON, N.C. ( InvestigateTV ) — Some doctors and caregivers are using art to help people with memory loss stay calm, engaged and connected. Research published by the National Library of Medicine shows drawing and painting can sometimes stimulate memories in people with dementia and other neurological diseases. Mother and daughter paint together June Lederle and her daughter, Cathie Lederle, create artwork at a table in their Wilmington home most days. On the day of the interview, Cathie was painting a bottle purple, the color of Alzheimer’s awareness. Before moving in with her mother, Cathie lived in Richmond, Virginia, and had a career in a technical field. June said the first signs that something was wrong appeared in 2019, starting with forgetfulness and then repeating tasks. Cognitive testing later confirmed their fears. According to Alaska State Troopers, 38-year-old Sasha Hart and her husband, 41-year-old David Hart, were killed in the Oct. 19 crash on the Parks Highway near Trapper Creek. items.t: Waco police investigating deadly pedestrian crash
items.x: WACO, Texas (KWTX) - Waco police are investigating after a 42-year-old man was struck and killed by two vehicles Thursday evening. Officers responded to the 2700 block of Robinson Drive around 7:40 p.m. for a report of a fatal pedestrian crash. According to investigators, the man was walking in the roadway when two vehicles struck him. The man was pronounced dead at the scene. His identity has not been released pending notification of next of kin. Police said both drivers remained at the scene and are cooperating with investigators. The investigation remains ongoing.

items.t: Older adults who stop driving face transportation gaps, experts say
items.x: KANSAS CITY ( InvestigateTV ) — As people age and their health changes, families can face the question of when a loved one should stop driving. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration reports older drivers are more likely than younger drivers to be involved in a car accident. They are “more likely to be seriously hurt,” according to the agency. Most older drivers do not have a plan for when they can no longer drive, which aging experts say is critical. A trip to the doctor without a car Kennie Sandbothe, 77, stopped driving and now relies on a ride program for older adults. Sandbothe was headed to a doctor’s appointment about 25 minutes from their home outside Kansas City. “There’s no buses out here, not in this kind of rural area out here,” Sandbothe said. “It’s so expensive for Uber to take somewhere all the time.” Sandbothe said they have thought about improvising. “Sometim

items.x: ( InvestigateTV ) — A new report from Environment America found bacteria levels were potentially unsafe on at least one day at 69% of more than 4,500 river and lake testing locations in 17 states. items.t: Doctor says time outdoors can support physical and mental health
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Spending time in nature can be a healthy reset, according to a doctor who also practices wilderness medicine. Dr. Nathaniel Mann, a Prisma Health emergency doctor, said time spent outdoors is one of the most powerful treatments he has seen, and he supports prescribing it. “Humans, we really didn’t evolve to live in these big structured communities with all the traffic and lights and noise. Our genetic roots are in the outdoors and the surroundings that we see around us right now,” Mann said. Doctor cites human history outdoors Mann spent two years traveling the world, practicing medicine in remote environments. Across his years in medicine, he has found that being outside is one of the most powerful treatments. items.t: Customers suffer chemical burns after drinking margaritas at a NC Chili’s, officials say
items.x: FOREST CITY, N.C. ( WHNS /Gray News) – A round of drinks turned into a medical nightmare when three customers ordered margaritas and immediately suffered chemical burns inside and around their mouths. Health officials investigating the incident at a Chili’s Grill & Bar in Forest City, North Carolina, said the drinks were contaminated after a powerful industrial degreaser was mistaken for sugar. The dangerous mix-up began when a restaurant worker obtained granulated degreasing agent from an outside contractor power-washing the building’s exterior, according to the Foothills Health District. The employee poured the chemical into an unlabeled container, brought it inside and left it in the bar area. items.t: City-owned vehicle crashes into former restaurant in Hazard
items.x: HAZARD, Ky. (WYMT/WKYT) - Police and paramedics were called to the former France’s Diner in downtown Hazard after a truck crashed into the building Friday morning. According to the building’s owner, the truck was owned and operated by the City of Hazard. The truck slammed into the building around 9:15 a.m. There was no one inside the building at the time of impact. There is no official word on the condition of the driver or the cause of the crash.

items.t: Older adults who stop driving face transportation gaps, experts say
items.x: KANSAS CITY ( InvestigateTV ) — As people age and their health changes, families can face the question of when a loved one should stop driving. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration reports older drivers are more likely than younger drivers to be involved in a car accident. They are “more likely to be seriously hurt,” according to the agency. Most older drivers do not have a plan for when they can no longer drive, which aging experts say is critical. A trip to the doctor without a car Kennie Sandbothe, 77, stopped driving and now relies on a ride program for older adults. Sandbothe was headed to a doctor’s appointment about 25 minutes from their home outside Kansas City. “There’s no buses out here, not in this kind of rural area out here,” Sandbothe said. “It’s so expensive for Uber to take somewhere all the time.” Sandbothe said they have thought about improvising. “Sometim

items.t: Doctor says time outdoors can support physical and mental health
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Spending time in nature can be a healthy reset, according to a doctor who also practices wilderness medicine. Dr. Nathaniel Mann, a Prisma Health emergency doctor, said time spent outdoors is one of the most powerful treatments he has seen, and he supports prescribing it. “Humans, we really didn’t evolve to live in these big structured communities with all the traffic and lights and noise. Our genetic roots are in the outdoors and the surroundings that we see around us right now,” Mann said. Doctor cites human history outdoors Mann spent two years traveling the world, practicing medicine in remote environments. Across his years in medicine, he has found that being outside is one of the most powerful treatments. items.x: FOREST CITY, N.C. ( WHNS /Gray News) – A round of drinks turned into a medical nightmare when three customers ordered margaritas and immediately suffered chemical burns inside and around their mouths. Health officials investigating the incident at a Chili’s Grill & Bar in Forest City, North Carolina, said the drinks were contaminated after a powerful industrial degreaser was mistaken for sugar. The employee poured the chemical into an unlabeled container, brought it inside and left it in the bar area. items.t: Dating again? What older adults should know about sexual health and protection
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Dating, intimacy and connection can be an important part of emotional and physical well-being for older adults. That includes people who are divorced, widowed, remarried or dating again for the first time in decades. The Aging Untold experts are addressing the topics of sexual health, how it has changed over the years and how to stay protected. items.t: Ground cinnamon recalled ahead of holiday season due to elevated lead risk, FDA says
items.x: (Gray News) - Ground cinnamon is being recalled in 14 states ahead of the holiday season. SLR Food Distribution Inc said it’s voluntarily recalling Wise Wife Brand Ground Cinnamon because it could be contaminated with elevated levels of lead, according to a recall alert. The affected cinnamon was sold in retail and grocery stores between Sept. 8, 2025, and June 28, 2026, in Connecticut, Indiana, Kansas, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, North Carolina, Nebraska, New York, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Texas, Virginia and Wisconsin. According to the recall notice, lead exposure can impact nearly every bodily system, with effects depending on dosage, duration, and an individual’s age and weight. Low-level, short-term exposure may not produce immediate symptoms, and no illnesses have been reported to date. items.t: When ‘I’ll never put you in a home’ meets real-life caregiving
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Caregiving promises are sometimes made during emotional moments. When a loved one says, “I’ll never put you in a home,” or “You can always live with me,” the words may come from love, but health, safety, money and caregiver capacity can change over time. The Aging Untold experts explain why families may feel guilt or pressure later and what to say instead. Why promises can create pressure Families often make promises before they have talked through what caregiving could involve, Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, said. “They haven’t looked at the reality and talked about the reality at first,” O’Rourke said. “You know, ‘I’ll take care of you.’ But if these certain things happen, we’re going to have to have another conversation.” She said the questions can be practical: Can we afford the care? items.t: ‘Bad houseguest’ in the attic: What to know about shingles symptoms and treatments
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Many people think the first sign of shingles is a bad rash, but it can start with intense pain in the body. ‘Intense amount of burning’ Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said she had shingles twice and it was tied to an autoimmune condition, and described the pain as burning. “It burned. It’s an infection in the nerve, essentially. It is nerve pain at the highest level,” Cradduck said. She compared it to a toothache. “You know how intense a toothache is. Now think about that in a pathway, in a nerve pathway in your body,” Cradduck said. Her pain was on her back and flank. “Not something I could see, not something I could reach, but just an intense amount of burning. And then it came around,” she said. items.t: Better than blood? Researcher says new discovery could help save lives
items.x: KANSAS CITY, Mo. ( InvestigateTV ) — A doctor and research scientist at the University of Missouri-Kansas City said he has discovered a potential alternative to blood transfusions for people with severe blood loss. He calls the treatment “better than blood.” When someone experiences severe trauma, such as a car crash or gunshot wound, they risk bleeding to death. Blood transfusions are currently the best treatment to try to stop severe blood loss, also known as hemorrhagic shock. How the discovery happened Dr. Cuthbert Simpkins, founder of Vivacelle Bio, said he was running an experiment he thought would fail. “But it didn’t fail.” For years, Simpkins, who is now a surgery professor at the UKMC School of Medicine, had been trying to find an answer for septic shock and focused his research on blood experiments. items.t: Consistent routine emphasized with adjustment to end of daylight saving time
items.x: WICHITA, Kan. (KWCH) - Daylight saving time ends Sunday, with clocks rolling back in the early-morning hours. Ahead of the change, staff at Wichita’s TMJ & Sleep Therapy Centre said sticking with a good sleep routine is the best way to adjust to the change. Experts point out that while the fall time change is easier to manage than the spring change, seniors and children may want to make a few adjustments to their bedtime routines. “If they stay consistent on a schedule or a routine, it does help them adapt to a change,” said TMJ & Sleep Therapy Centre Clinical Assistant Tida Huynh. “When we’re treating kids, we typically recommend For children ahead of a time change, TMJ & Sleep Therapy recommends shifting bedtime by 10 minutes at a time throughout the week. items.t: How caregivers can keep dignity intact when conversations get tense
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Stress can turn into sharp words when you are a caregiver for someone you love. The Aging Untold experts are sharing advice on how to communicate in a way that keeps dignity intact, builds cooperation and helps caregivers reset when a conversation escalates. Step away before things escalate “Sam” Cradduck, a gerontologist, said the first move to make when it feels like a conversation is about to escalate is to leave the room. “You have to step away. You really do,” Cradduck said. “You’ve got to let yourself calm down.” Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said caregivers can take that step by removing themselves or getting help. “If you’re fantasizing about escaping, or noticing the yellow flags like you’re starting to get hot, shaky, your jaw’s tense, that’s a good time to go, ‘OK, my nervous system is at its limit,’” Ambrose said. items.t: Man charged in Oct. 2 fatal accident gets judge changed in case
items.x: BISMARCK, N.D. (KFYR) - A Bismarck man facing criminal charges following a fatal accident on Oct. 2 that killed two teenagers is getting a new judge on his case. Court documents show Cameron Schestler’s defense attorney filed a demand to disqualify District Judge James Hill, which has now been approved. Under North Dakota law, defendants can request a one-time change of judge before key rulings are made in the case. According to the court record, the case is reassigned to Judge Bobbi Weiler in the Burleigh County Courts.

items.t: Older adults who stop driving face transportation gaps, experts say
items.x: KANSAS CITY ( InvestigateTV ) — As people age and their health changes, families can face the question of when a loved one should stop driving. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration reports older drivers are more likely than younger drivers to be involved in a car accident. They are “more likely to be seriously hurt,” according to the agency. Most older drivers do not have a plan for when they can no longer drive, which aging experts say is critical. items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Spending time in nature can be a healthy reset, according to a doctor who also practices wilderness medicine. Dr. Nathaniel Mann, a Prisma Health emergency doctor, said time spent outdoors is one of the most powerful treatments he has seen, and he supports prescribing it. “Humans, we really didn’t evolve to live in these big structured communities with all the traffic and lights and noise. ( WHNS /Gray News) – A round of drinks turned into a medical nightmare when three customers ordered margaritas and immediately suffered chemical burns inside and around their mouths. The employee poured the chemical into an unlabeled container, brought it inside and left it in the bar area. items.t: Ground cinnamon recalled ahead of holiday season due to elevated lead risk, FDA says
items.x: (Gray News) - Ground cinnamon is being recalled in 14 states ahead of the holiday season. SLR Food Distribution Inc said it’s voluntarily recalling Wise Wife Brand Ground Cinnamon because it could be contaminated with elevated levels of lead, according to a recall alert. The affected cinnamon was sold in retail and grocery stores between Sept. 8, 2025, and June 28, 2026, in Connecticut, Indiana, Kansas, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, North Carolina, Nebraska, New York, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Texas, Virginia and Wisconsin. According to the recall notice, lead exposure can impact nearly every bodily system, with effects depending on dosage, duration, and an individual’s age and weight. Low-level, short-term exposure may not produce immediate symptoms, and no illnesses have been reported to date. According to Alaska State Troopers, 38-year-old Sasha Hart and her husband, 41-year-old David Hart, were killed in the Oct. 19 crash on the Parks Highway near Trapper Creek. According to troopers, Sasha Hart was driving a Subaru Forester south on the Parks Highway when she crossed the center line and collided head-on with a northbound Ford F-250. Their 2-year-old daughter, Paige, was also in the Subaru and survived. “She’s a miracle. Aren’t you?” Shery Elterman-Hart, David Hart’s sister, said as she held her niece during an interview. A life built in Fairbanks According to the Hart family, the couple just celebrated their 10-year anniversary. items.t: Exonerated man calls for prison reform at Binghamton University event
items.x: BINGHAMTON, N.Y. (WBNG) - Marvin Anderson, who was wrongfully convicted of sexual crimes at age 18 and sentenced to 210 years in prison, spoke Thursday morning at Binghamton University’s Downtown Center about reforming the prison system. Conviction and exoneration An all-white jury convicted Anderson in 1982. He was exonerated after 20 years with help from the Innocence Project, an organization he is now part of. Anderson described the day of the verdict. “That day in the courtroom, I was found guilty. The whole room just went dark. I couldn’t see my family. And they were sitting directly behind me. And I just sensed that, you know, my life was over,” Anderson said. Calls for reform Anderson spoke to a crowd about changes to the prison system. “Our justice system is broken… All they know is build more prison, build more prison, but no one is trying to solve the problem,” Anderson said. ( WHNS /Gray News) – A round of drinks turned into a medical nightmare when three customers ordered margaritas and immediately suffered chemical burns inside and around their mouths. The employee poured the chemical into an unlabeled container, brought it inside and left it in the bar area. items.t: Dating again? What older adults should know about sexual health and protection
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Dating, intimacy and connection can be an important part of emotional and physical well-being for older adults. That includes people who are divorced, widowed, remarried or dating again for the first time in decades. The Aging Untold experts are addressing the topics of sexual health, how it has changed over the years and how to stay protected. items.t: Ground cinnamon recalled ahead of holiday season due to elevated lead risk, FDA says
items.x: (Gray News) - Ground cinnamon is being recalled in 14 states ahead of the holiday season. SLR Food Distribution Inc said it’s voluntarily recalling Wise Wife Brand Ground Cinnamon because it could be contaminated with elevated levels of lead, according to a recall alert. The affected cinnamon was sold in retail and grocery stores between Sept. 8, 2025, and June 28, 2026, in Connecticut, Indiana, Kansas, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, North Carolina, Nebraska, New York, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Texas, Virginia and Wisconsin. According to the recall notice, lead exposure can impact nearly every bodily system, with effects depending on dosage, duration, and an individual’s age and weight. Low-level, short-term exposure may not produce immediate symptoms, and no illnesses have been reported to date. items.t: When ‘I’ll never put you in a home’ meets real-life caregiving
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Caregiving promises are sometimes made during emotional moments. When a loved one says, “I’ll never put you in a home,” or “You can always live with me,” the words may come from love, but health, safety, money and caregiver capacity can change over time. The Aging Untold experts explain why families may feel guilt or pressure later and what to say instead. items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Many people think the first sign of shingles is a bad rash, but it can start with intense pain in the body. ‘Intense amount of burning’ Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said she had shingles twice and it was tied to an autoimmune condition, and described the pain as burning. “It burned. It’s an infection in the nerve, essentially. It is nerve pain at the highest level,” Cradduck said. She compared it to a toothache. “You know how intense a toothache is. Now think about that in a pathway, in a nerve pathway in your body,” Cradduck said. Her pain was on her back and flank. “Not something I could see, not something I could reach, but just an intense amount of burning. And then it came around,” she said. items.t: Better than blood? Researcher says new discovery could help save lives
items.x: KANSAS CITY, Mo. ( InvestigateTV ) — A doctor and research scientist at the University of Missouri-Kansas City said he has discovered a potential alternative to blood transfusions for people with severe blood loss. He calls the treatment “better than blood.” When someone experiences severe trauma, such as a car crash or gunshot wound, they risk bleeding to death. Blood transfusions are currently the best treatment to try to stop severe blood loss, also known as hemorrhagic shock. items.t: How caregivers can keep dignity intact when conversations get tense
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Stress can turn into sharp words when you are a caregiver for someone you love. The Aging Untold experts are sharing advice on how to communicate in a way that keeps dignity intact, builds cooperation and helps caregivers reset when a conversation escalates. Step away before things escalate “Sam” Cradduck, a gerontologist, said the first move to make when it feels like a conversation is about to escalate is to leave the room. “You have to step away. You really do,” Cradduck said. “You’ve got to let yourself calm down.” Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said caregivers can take that step by removing themselves or getting help. “If you’re fantasizing about escaping, or noticing the yellow flags like you’re starting to get hot, shaky, your jaw’s tense, that’s a good time to go, ‘OK, my nervous system is at its limit,’” Ambrose said. items.t: What to look for in a clinical trial and why older adults should be included
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Clinical trials can be a proactive way to explore new treatments, but studies show older adults are often left out of them, even though many conditions affect older adults more often. The Aging Untold experts hosts are discussing what to look for when choosing a study and how to decide whether to take part. items.t: Bringing cancer screening conversations to the salon chair
items.x: ANDRESON, S.C. ( InvestigateTV ) - Do you only go to the doctor when you have an ache or feel sick? For many women that answer can be “yes.” A 2025 survey said that every one in six women say they missed or may have missed a routine cancer screening within the past year. A South Carolina salon is partnering with a statewide health initiative to have important conversations about cancer screening with clients. Kimberly Cheatham, owner of Kreative Kimistry in Anderson, has joined the Pink Palmetto Project, an effort by the South Carolina Cancer Alliance focusing on breast and cervical cancer education. Cheatham said her clients often get personal with her. “They confide in me when they don’t even feel comfortable telling their families things and their friends, because they know that I have a connection to them,” Cheatham said. ( InvestigateTV ) — A 1-year-old dog named Blueberry and a 10-month-old cat named Meadow were adopted together after they met at the veterinary hospital run by Last Chance Animal Rescue in Waldorf, Maryland. Hospital Manager Lauren Webb said she got a call about Blueberry on Christmas Eve. “We’ve got to help this dog. It’s Christmas Eve. We’ve got to pull out a miracle,” Webb recalled. items.t: How art therapy helps patients connect with caregivers
items.x: WILMINGTON, N.C. ( InvestigateTV ) — Some doctors and caregivers are using art to help people with memory loss stay calm, engaged and connected. Research published by the National Library of Medicine shows drawing and painting can sometimes stimulate memories in people with dementia and other neurological diseases. Mother and daughter paint together June Lederle and her daughter, Cathie Lederle, create artwork at a table in their Wilmington home most days. On the day of the interview, Cathie was painting a bottle purple, the color of Alzheimer’s awareness. Before moving in with her mother, Cathie lived in Richmond, Virginia, and had a career in a technical field. June said the first signs that something was wrong appeared in 2019, starting with forgetfulness and then repeating tasks. Cognitive testing later confirmed their fears. items.t: Deputies: Strasburg man dies after speeding away from traffic stop, crashing
items.x: MASSILLON, Ohio (WOIO) - Stark County deputies are investigating after a man reportedly fled a traffic stop by Massillon police and crashed, leading to his death. According to deputies, officers with Massillon police attempted to pull over a vehicle around 12:30 a.m. Friday in the of 17th Street SW and Finefrock Road SW. However instead of stopping, the driver sped away, the sheriff’s office said in a news release. Officers tried to catch up and found the vehicle crashed near 4600 block of Carmont Avenue SW in Tuscarawas Township. Deputies said first responders pronounced the driver, Shawn Honaker, 41, of Strasburg, dead at the scene. No one else was hurt. The Stark County Sheriff’s Office is handling the investigation.

items.t: Ohio bill aims to protect police officers’ private information from being posted online
items.x: CLEVELAND, Ohio (WOIO) - A new bill introduced in the Ohio Statehouse aims to protect peace officers and their families from having their personal information published online. State Rep. Gayle Manning (R-North Ridgeville) sponsored the measure after the Lorain Police Department approached her about an incident where an officer faced intense, nationwide backlash online despite being cleared of any wrongdoing. “They were found they had not done anything wrong, but then that information goes viral,” Manning said. “And all of a sudden, because of social media, it was all over the United States.” Under the proposed legislation, it would be illegal to publicly disclose an officer’s personal identifying information—such as a home address, birth date, or phone number—with the intent to intimidate, threaten, or cause physical harm. items.t: Arraignment for former Northeast Ohio high school band director indicted by grand jury
items.x: STARK COUNTY, Ohio (WOIO) — The former band director at Northwest High School in Canal Fulton was arraigned in Stark County Court of Common Pleas Friday. Stephen Imler pleaded not guilty to three charges of sexual battery and one charge of grooming. The judge set bond at $200,000 and ordered Imler to return to court on Nov. 12. Imler, who was also a music teacher at the high school, was placed on administrative leave on Aug. 18 when the allegations were first announced. On Sept. 2, Imler officially resigned from both positions. He was arrested by members of the U.S. Marshals Northern Ohio Violent Fugitive Task Force on Oct. 23. According to U.S. Marshal Pete Elliott, Imler was taken into custody without incident at a home in the 4600 block of Hametown Rd. in Norton.

items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Stress can turn into sharp words when you are a caregiver for someone you love. The Aging Untold experts are sharing advice on how to communicate in a way that keeps dignity intact, builds cooperation and helps caregivers reset when a conversation escalates. items.x: KANSAS CITY ( InvestigateTV ) — As people age and their health changes, families can face the question of when a loved one should stop driving. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration reports older drivers are more likely than younger drivers to be involved in a car accident. items.x: COLUMBIA, S.C. (WIS) - Fear is instilled in all of us, but it varies from person to person. Like most reactions, fear starts in the brain. Your amygdala, located behind your eyes and between your ears, is an almond-shaped cluster of cells. It’s a primary emotional processor, picking up on other emotions and linking them to different senses, including fear. Historically, humans have needed fear to avoid danger altogether and survive. Some fears and anxieties can be genetic, but the situation controls your emotions. Let’s say you’re on the riverwalk and you encounter a bear. Immediately, your amygdala gets to work, signaling your hypothalamus to produce stress hormones such as adrenaline. Simultaneously, your hippocampus triggers a “fight or flight” response. items.t: Older adults who stop driving face transportation gaps, experts say
items.x: KANSAS CITY ( InvestigateTV ) — As people age and their health changes, families can face the question of when a loved one should stop driving. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration reports older drivers are more likely than younger drivers to be involved in a car accident. They are “more likely to be seriously hurt,” according to the agency. Most older drivers do not have a plan for when they can no longer drive, which aging experts say is critical. A trip to the doctor without a car Kennie Sandbothe, 77, stopped driving and now relies on a ride program for older adults. Dr. Nathaniel Mann, a Prisma Health emergency doctor, said time spent outdoors is one of the most powerful treatments he has seen, and he supports prescribing it. “Humans, we really didn’t evolve to live in these big structured communities with all the traffic and lights and noise. Doctor cites human history outdoors Mann spent two years traveling the world, practicing medicine in remote environments. Across his years in medicine, he has found that being outside is one of the most powerful treatments. When a loved one says, “I’ll never put you in a home,” or “You can always live with me,” the words may come from love, but health, safety, money and caregiver capacity can change over time. It’s an infection in the nerve, essentially. It is nerve pain at the highest level,” Cradduck said. She compared it to a toothache. “You know how intense a toothache is. Now think about that in a pathway, in a nerve pathway in your body,” Cradduck said. Her pain was on her back and flank. “Not something I could see, not something I could reach, but just an intense amount of burning. And then it came around,” she said. items.x: KANSAS CITY, Mo. ( InvestigateTV ) — A doctor and research scientist at the University of Missouri-Kansas City said he has discovered a potential alternative to blood transfusions for people with severe blood loss. He calls the treatment “better than blood.” When someone experiences severe trauma, such as a car crash or gunshot wound, they risk bleeding to death. items.t: How caregivers can keep dignity intact when conversations get tense
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Stress can turn into sharp words when you are a caregiver for someone you love. The Aging Untold experts are sharing advice on how to communicate in a way that keeps dignity intact, builds cooperation and helps caregivers reset when a conversation escalates. Step away before things escalate “Sam” Cradduck, a gerontologist, said the first move to make when it feels like a conversation is about to escalate is to leave the room. “You have to step away. You really do,” Cradduck said. “You’ve got to let yourself calm down.” Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said caregivers can take that step by removing themselves or getting help. “If you’re fantasizing about escaping, or noticing the yellow flags like you’re starting to get hot, shaky, your jaw’s tense, that’s a good time to go, ‘OK, my nervous system is at its limit,’” Ambrose said. items.t: Georgetown County deputies end search for missing, endangered man
items.x: GEORGETOWN COUNTY, S.C. (WCSC) — The Georgetown County Sheriff’s Office has ceased the search for a man who was reported missing by his family. Deputies said 57-year-old Christopher Todd Harms stopped communicating with his family last week Friday. He had moved out of his home on Massick Lane on Pawleys Island two weeks prior, but had kept in touch by phone. He was also reportedly in a heightened emotional state. “The Sheriff’s Office is saddened to report that the search for Christopher Harms, missing from Pawleys Island, is over. It is not the outcome we wanted or expected, but the family and the Sheriff’s Office wants to thank everyone for their efforts in the search. We send our condolences and ask that the family’s request for time to grieve in private is respected,” spokesperson Heather Pelham said Friday morning.

The lineup includes: Welcome and closing remarks: Jason Bocchino, retired U.S. Navy and CFCC director of veteran services Pledge of Allegiance: Trefor Hopkins, U.S. Marine Corps Presentation of colors and national anthem: H&S Battalion Color Guard, U.S. Marine Corps Invocation: Richard Whaley, retired U.S. Army Opening remarks: Jim Morton, CFCC president Reading of “I am a Veteran”: Bianca Kyle, U.S. Army Keynote address: Dr. Lauren Tidwell, U.S. Army veteran and CFCC dean of career and technical education Service hymns: Michael Guay, U.S. Marine Corps Student speaker: Sonya Ford, U.S. Navy POW

items.t: InvestigateTV+: Prison program helping veterans
items.x: ( InvestigateTV ) — InvestigateTV+ takes you inside a peer-led prison program helping incarcerated veterans rebuild purpose through discipline and mentorship and talk to the supporters who say it’s breaking the cycle. Plus, how art is helping dementia patients reconnect and communicate. Then, an unlikely dog-and-cat friendship brings comfort to one family. Helping veterans rebuild American Legion Veterans Memorial Post 432 at Elayn Hunt Correctional Center was the first prison-based American Legion post in Louisiana, helping incarcerated veterans heal and rebuild their lives. The program is recognized for a zero percent recidivism rate. No one from the post comes back to prison. items.t: Bringing cancer screening conversations to the salon chair
items.x: ANDRESON, S.C. ( InvestigateTV ) - Do you only go to the doctor when you have an ache or feel sick? For many women that answer can be “yes.” A 2025 survey said that every one in six women say they missed or may have missed a routine cancer screening within the past year. A South Carolina salon is partnering with a statewide health initiative to have important conversations about cancer screening with clients. Kimberly Cheatham, owner of Kreative Kimistry in Anderson, has joined the Pink Palmetto Project, an effort by the South Carolina Cancer Alliance focusing on breast and cervical cancer education. Cheatham said her clients often get personal with her. “They confide in me when they don’t even feel comfortable telling their families things and their friends, because they know that I have a connection to them,” Cheatham said. items.t: The three-legged cat and dog duo that are best friends
items.x: WALDORF, Md. ( InvestigateTV ) — A 1-year-old dog named Blueberry and a 10-month-old cat named Meadow were adopted together after they met at the veterinary hospital run by Last Chance Animal Rescue in Waldorf, Maryland. Rachel Clarke, who adopted both animals, said Blueberry “loves to play, and she loves to snuggle.” She said Meadow is “a little more independent, but Blueberry goes where Meadow goes.” Laurie Jenkins, assistant director of Last Chance Animal Rescue, said both animals arrived with wounds to their extremities that required amputations. Hospital Manager Lauren Webb said she got a call about Blueberry on Christmas Eve. “We’ve got to help this dog. It’s Christmas Eve. We’ve got to pull out a miracle,” Webb recalled. items.t: How art therapy helps patients connect with caregivers
items.x: WILMINGTON, N.C. ( InvestigateTV ) — Some doctors and caregivers are using art to help people with memory loss stay calm, engaged and connected. Research published by the National Library of Medicine shows drawing and painting can sometimes stimulate memories in people with dementia and other neurological diseases. Mother and daughter paint together June Lederle and her daughter, Cathie Lederle, create artwork at a table in their Wilmington home most days. On the day of the interview, Cathie was painting a bottle purple, the color of Alzheimer’s awareness. Before moving in with her mother, Cathie lived in Richmond, Virginia, and had a career in a technical field. June said the first signs that something was wrong appeared in 2019, starting with forgetfulness and then repeating tasks. Cognitive testing later confirmed their fears. items.t: Pet of the Week: Meet Tiana from Paws Place Dog Rescue
items.x: WILMINGTON, N.C. (WECT) - A 1 1/2-year-old shepherd mix named Tiana is waiting to meet her forever family at Paws Place Dog Rescue. Staff describe Tiana as an energetic, affectionate companion who knows tricks and enjoys splashing around in the facility’s doggie pool. She is equally comfortable joining a multi-dog household or thriving as an only pet, and rescue workers say she gets along well with both adults and children. Those interested in adopting can visit the rescue facility at 242 George II Highway in Winnabow. Walk-ins are welcome Tuesday through Saturday from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m., with no appointment necessary. For more details on the adoption process, call Paws Place Dog Rescue at 910-845-7297.

items.t: ‘She’s a miracle’: Family says 2-year-old is healing after crash that killed her parents
items.x: ANCHORAGE, Alaska ( KTUU /Gray News) — A fatal head-on collision on an Alaska highway last week killed a Fairbanks couple. According to Alaska State Troopers, 38-year-old Sasha Hart and her husband, 41-year-old David Hart, were killed in the Oct. 19 crash on the Parks Highway near Trapper Creek. According to troopers, Sasha Hart was driving a Subaru Forester south on the Parks Highway when she crossed the center line and collided head-on with a northbound Ford F-250. Their 2-year-old daughter, Paige, was also in the Subaru and survived. “She’s a miracle. Aren’t you?” Shery Elterman-Hart, David Hart’s sister, said as she held her niece during an interview. A life built in Fairbanks According to the Hart family, the couple just celebrated their 10-year anniversary. items.t: First Alert Forecast: an eerie change for Halloween weekend
items.x: WILMINGTON, N.C. (WECT) - Friday and Halloween Saturday will have mild and misty mornings, warm and brisk afternoons, and no rain-- You’re welcome trick-or-treaters! Don’t forget to set your manual clocks back an hour Saturday night as Daylight Saving Time comes to an end in the week hours of Sunday, November 1. It is also a good opportunity to change batteries in your smoke detectors and CO detectors. Speaking of early November, balmy breezes will whisk in the Cape Fear’s next best rain chances; Election Day Tuesday should fare dry, but Wednesday to Friday has the highest odds as of now. Significant shower and thunderstorms activity is increasingly likely on Thursday. Prospects for a widespread frost or freeze are slim to none until the middle of the month, at the earliest. items.t: 3 dead in Oregon helicopter collision, including flight instructor and student pilot
items.x: MCMINNVILLE, Ore. ( KPTV /Gray News) — Three people are dead after two helicopters crashed into each other Thursday afternoon near an Oregon airport, officials said. Crash location and road closure The Yamhill County Sheriff’s Office said the crash was reported around 2:15 p.m. near Lafayette Highway and Southeast Stringtown Road. The crash scene is near McMinnville Municipal Airport, southeast of McMinnville. Aircraft involved The two helicopters were identified as an Airbus Helicopters AS350B2 and a Robinson R22, according to the NTSB. Jerry Trimble Helicopters, a flight training company, posted on social media that one of its aircraft was involved in the crash. Photos show the aftermath of a deadly helicopter collision in near an Oregon airport.
